t: Smallest K-Length Subsequence With Occurrences of a Letter - Greedy Stack with Quota Guards
o: We must keep exactly k characters of s (order preserved) so that the given letter appears at least repetition times, and among all valid candidates pick the lexicographically smallest one. For s = "leet", k = 3, repetition = 1, the valid length-3 subsequences containing 'e' are "lee", "let" and "eet", so "eet" wins even though it means discarding the early 'l'. Since s can be up to 5 * 10^4 characters, trying every C(n, k) combination is hopeless; we need a linear greedy. The tests guarantee at least one valid subsequence exists.
k: A monotonic stack greedily builds the lexicographically smallest subsequence of length k: a new smaller character pops larger tops while the remaining characters still allow reaching length k.
The letter quota adds two guards: never pop a letter unless later occurrences can repay the quota, and never spend a slot on a non-letter if the still-required letters could no longer fit.
Precomputing suffix counts of the required letter makes both feasibility checks O(1), keeping the whole scan linear.

a.i: Translate the statement literally: generate every way to choose k indices in increasing order, keep those whose characters contain letter at least repetition times, and remember the smallest string seen. Obviously correct and astronomically slow at the given limits; it pins down the semantics.
s: Recursively extend a selection starting from index start until k indices are chosen.
Count occurrences of letter in the built string.
If the count reaches repetition, compare the string with the best so far.
Return the best after all combinations are exhausted.
a.t: Exponential - explores roughly C(n, k) index combinations with O(k) work each; hopeless at |s| = 5 * 10^4.
a.sp: O(k) - recursion depth and the current candidate string.

a.n: Approach 2: Greedy Monotonic Stack with Quota Guards
a.i: Build the answer left to right in a stack. When the incoming character is smaller than the stack top, popping that top improves the result, provided length k is still reachable afterwards: len(stack) - 1 + (n - i) >= k (the incoming character itself counts among the remaining n - i). The quota injects two extra conditions: popping a stacked letter requires cnt - 1 + suffix[i] >= repetition, and pushing a non-letter is forbidden when repetition - cnt > k - len(stack) - 1, i.e., when it would crowd out letters we are still obliged to include. suffix[i] counts occurrences of letter in s[i:], so every check is constant time.
s: Precompute suffix[i] = number of occurrences of letter in s[i:]; track cnt = letters currently in the stack.
Scan i left to right; while the top exceeds s[i] AND len(stack) + n - i - 1 >= k AND cnt - isTopLetter + suffix[i] >= repetition, pop.
If the stack holds fewer than k characters, push s[i].
Before pushing a non-letter, additionally require repetition - cnt <= k - len(stack) - 1.
Join the stack and return it.
a.t: O(n) - each character enters and leaves the stack at most once, with O(1) work per move.
a.sp: O(n) - the suffix array; the stack itself never exceeds k characters.

w: Derive the plain smallest-subsequence-of-length-k stack greedy first, then layer in the two quota guards one at a time - reciting four conditions up front reads poorly in an interview. Common bugs: forgetting that the incoming character counts toward remaining capacity (use n - i, not n - i - 1), popping a letter the suffix cannot repay, and filling all k slots with non-letters. Test s = "bb", k = 2, repetition = 2 (forced full-quota answer) and cases where 2d... rather, where repetition equals the total supply of the letter. Follow-ups: require exactly repetition occurrences (also cap pushes of the letter), or satisfy several constrained letters at once.
